lesson.title: Ripples Through the Food Web: Trophic Cascades
lesson.summary: A trophic cascade occurs when a change at one trophic level, often a change in predator numbers, ripples down through the food chain to affect the levels below it, sometimes reshaping an entire ecosystem.
lesson.body:
You have already learned about trophic levels and food chains and food webs, the layered structure of who eats whom in a community, from producers up through primary, secondary, and sometimes tertiary consumers. A trophic cascade is what happens when a change at one level of that structure, usually a change in the abundance of a predator, triggers a chain reaction of effects that ripple down through the levels beneath it. The keystone species examples from the last chapter are really trophic cascades in action: when sea otters are removed, urchins increase, and kelp declines, a change flowing from the top predator level down through the herbivore level to the producer level.

That three level otter, urchin, kelp system is one of the cleanest, most direct examples of a trophic cascade that ecologists point to, precisely because the otter's effect on the kelp is indirect, working entirely through its effect on the urchins in between. Removing the top predator does not touch the kelp directly at all, and yet the kelp forest can collapse anyway, simply because the level in between it and the predator has been released from control.

A more complicated and more debated case is the reintroduction of gray wolves to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, after decades of the park having no wolf population. Some researchers have reported that, following the wolves' return, elk behavior and elk numbers changed in ways that reduced browsing pressure on young willow and aspen trees in certain areas, allowing some streamside vegetation to recover, with follow on effects proposed for species such as beavers and songbirds that depend on that vegetation. This example is often presented, including in popular science writing, as a clean, dramatic illustration of a trophic cascade reshaping an entire landscape. It is worth being cautious here, though: many ecologists who have studied the Yellowstone data closely argue that the story is considerably more complicated than that popular version suggests, since elk numbers were also affected by hunting outside the park, by drought and other climate factors, and by the presence of other predators, and the vegetation recovery has been uneven across different parts of the park rather than uniform. The wolf reintroduction remains a genuinely important and actively studied case, but it is best treated as an example of how trophic cascades can occur and how hard they can be to disentangle from other causes, rather than as a simple, fully settled proof of a single one directional cascade.

Trophic cascades do not always run from the top down, and they are not guaranteed to happen just because a predator is added or removed. Whether a cascade appears, and how strong it is, depends on the details of the food web involved, including how many species are present at each level and how strongly connected they are. Still, the underlying lesson connects back to the idea of keystone species: because organisms are linked together through feeding relationships, a change concentrated in just one part of a food web, especially at the predator level, can in principle spread outward and reshape levels that are not directly connected to it at all.
